passages: [prose] The study was carried out on old secondary or natural broad-leaved forests in the Shiiba Research Forest, Kyushu University (3221 0 N, 13105 0 E), the Kashiba National Forest (3221 0 N, 13112 0 E), and the Tano Forest Science Station, Miyazaki University (3151 0 N, 13117 0 E) in the Kyushu Central Mountains (Figure 1). We selected 11 sites at different elevations from 177 m above sea level (a.s.l.) to 1604 m a.s.l. in these areas (Table 1). The Tano forest (177 m a.s.l.) included evergreen broad-leaved trees such as Castanopsis sieboldii and C. cuspidata. The Kashiba forest (723, 787 m a.s.l.) included evergreen broad-leaved trees such as Quercus acta and Q. salicina. In the Shiiba forest (1068, 1095, 1187, 1209, 1249, 1410, 1483, and 1604 m a.s.l.), there are deciduous broad-leaved trees, such as Fagus crenata, Q. crispula, Acer sieboldianum, and Ac. pictum, and coniferous trees, including Abies firma. There is little understory vegetation (such as herbs, which are pollen resources) due to overgrazing by deer in Kashiba and Shiiba. [prose] Yellow pan traps were used for the sample collection (Figure 2). Pan traps have low human bias and are the most efficient and cost-effective methods for large-scale and longterm monitoring schemes with surveyors of different experience levels for all insect groups (Westphal et al., 2008). One limitation is that color preference differs depending on the species for all insect groups (Leong & Thorp, 1999), so that species that favor other colors may be under-sampled and their numbers underestimated. A yellow plastic bowl with a diameter of 15 cm was used. Each bowl was filled with approximately 150 ml of water with a few drops of dishwashing detergent as a surfactant.

[prose] We selected five functional traits that were expected to respond to elevational changes (body size, trophic level, feeding guild, flight duration, and elevational range) (Table S1). Body size was taken from the literature data of Tadauchi and Murao (2014) (for bees) and Terayama and Suda (2016) (for wasps). Trophic levels were defined at three levels: (1) herbivores (pollinator bees), (2) primary predators (predators and parasitoids of herbivores), and (3) secondary predators (predators and parasitoids of predators). Feeding guild was divided into four types that were classified according to the mechanism that adults use to feed their larvae: pollination, hunting, brood parasitism, and parasitoidism. The flight duration was calculated as the number of sampling times that the species was collected. The elevational range was calculated as the difference between the highest and lowest elevations at which the species was collected.
